paras: The lynching of Noah Taylor was the hanging of a Black man by a body of men who took him from the jail at Harrisonburg, Catahoula Parish, Louisiana, in December 1888. Taylor had been arrested as a suspect in the ambush killing of R. N. Stegall on a road below Harrisonburg a few days earlier. A Times-Democrat dispatch from Natchez carried the story to papers across the country, some of which set it against the news from Birmingham, Alabama, where a sheriff had defended his jail against a mob.

According to the Natchez Democrat, as reprinted in the Ouachita Telegraph of Monroe, Stegall had once worked as engineer at the Natchez ice factory and was living at or near Trinity when he rode to Harrisonburg on business on a Saturday. On his way home, about three miles below the town, he was shot from ambush with a shotgun and knocked from his horse, and the assassin then fired two revolver shots into his head before fleeing and leaving the shotgun behind. A dispatch dated Catahoula Parish, December 11, called the killing "cold blooded assassination" by "an unknown person." The Natchez Democrat said no motive had been ascribed and that "certain parties," said to have come over from Natchez, were suspected.

Searching parties, according to the Times-Democrat's Natchez special, followed a clue to Taylor's house, where they found a few articles Stegall had bought at Harrisonburg. Taylor's wife, "being closely questioned," made a statement that the dispatch said showed her husband had committed the killing; a shorter version printed in the Rock Island Argus said she "confessed" that he was the assassin. The Ouachita Telegraph said Taylor was arrested on suspicion the day after the murder, while the Diamond Drill of Crystal Falls, Michigan, said he was captured on Tuesday.

Taylor was held in the jail at Harrisonburg. On the night before the December 11 dispatch, "a body of men entered the jail, took Taylor and hanged him to a tree in the jail yard." The Argus version said the men "forced entrance," but no report names any of them, gives their number or describes what the sheriff did.
No report of an inquest, of arrests of the lynchers or of grand-jury action appears in the coverage.

The Times-Democrat's Natchez special ran on December 12 in the Savannah Morning News and the Richmond Dispatch, which headed it "Lynched by a Mob." Shorter versions appeared the same day in the Rock Island Daily Argus, the Sacramento Daily Record-Union and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer, and two days later in the Bismarck Weekly Tribune. The wire text called Taylor "the murderer," and the Seattle and Bismarck headlines read "Negro Murderer Lynched" and "Lynched the Murder."

Two headline writers read the story against events in Birmingham: the Savannah Morning News headed it "The Jail Entered Without Bloody Resistance by the Sheriff," and the Rock Island Argus "Not the Birmingham Style of Sheriff." Weekly summaries of the same weeks reported that Alabama's governor approved Sheriff Smith's defense of the Birmingham jail against a mob. The Sacramento Daily Record-Union titled its one-sentence brief "The Usual Southern 'Sequel.'"

Closer to the scene, the Ouachita Telegraph called Taylor "a worthless negro" and said he was lynched with "the evidence pointing to his guilt." Syndicated news summaries later in December cut the story to a single line; the Narragansett Herald and the Abbeville Press and Banner placed Harrisonburg in Mississippi. The Iowa Plain Dealer dated the lynching "on the 11th," and the Diamond Drill stated as fact that Taylor "killed R. N. Steagall." Papers spelled the dead man's name Stegall, Stegal and Steagall, and the Bismarck paper misprinted its dateline as "Nov. 11" and the town as "Harrisburg."

The Natchez special of December 11 placed the lynching on the previous night, while the Iowa Plain Dealer gave the 11th, a date that matches the dispatch date used throughout that summary. Most accounts put Stegall's murder on a Saturday night, but a Raymond Gazette item reprinted in the Greenville Times said he "was assassinated Monday."

accounts.gist: Searching parties followed a clue to Taylor's house, found articles Stegall had bought, and Taylor's wife made a statement implicating him; a body of men later entered the jail and hanged him to a tree in the jail yard.

accounts.label: Ouachita Telegraph (regional)
accounts.gist: After reprinting the Natchez Democrat's account of the assassination, the Monroe paper added that Taylor was arrested on suspicion the day after the murder and, with the evidence pointing to his guilt, was taken from jail and lynched by a mob.

accounts.label: Weekly news summaries
accounts.gist: One-line items reporting that a mob took Taylor from jail and hanged him, with varying dates and with the state given as Mississippi in some.

framing.detail: Wire text and headlines ('Negro Murderer Lynched', 'Lynched the Murder') call Taylor 'the murderer' without qualification.
Headlines set the lynching against the Birmingham jail defense: 'The Jail Entered Without Bloody Resistance by the Sheriff' and 'Not the Birmingham Style of Sheriff'.
The Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed its brief 'The Usual Southern "Sequel."', an ironic headline on Southern lynching.
The Ouachita Telegraph called Taylor 'a worthless negro' and said the evidence pointed to his guilt.

versions.value: Night of Dec. 10 ('last night' in Dec. 11 dispatch)

conflicts.note: The Dec. 11 dispatch is the most direct statement; the Iowa summary's date matches the dispatch date, as do other items in that summary. Research notes also report 'the 18th' in two unopened summaries (A14, A16), likely a misprint.
The Natchez special and the Natchez Democrat (via A11) both say Saturday; the Raymond Gazette item reprinted in A18 says Monday.
A1 says only that searching parties followed a clue to his house.
The Mississippi version appears only in a syndicated news summary and likely confuses the Natchez, Miss., dateline.
